Maintain
mayn-TAYN
v.t.
From Old French maintenir, from Latin manu tenere, to hold in the hand. Webster 1828: to hold or keep in any particular state; to support; to defend; to vindicate. Scripture uses it for two things: the cause of the afflicted, which God maintains, and good works, which the church must.

Biblical Definition

Twice in one short chapter Paul tells Titus that believers must maintain good works, and the repetition is deliberate: This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works (Titus 3:8), and again, let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful (Titus 3:14). The verb is not perform but maintain — to hold up, to keep going, to sustain as a settled occupation. And the placement is everything: it stands immediately after the strongest denial of works-righteousness in the epistle, that He saved us not by works of righteousness which we have done (Titus 3:5). God is said to maintain what men cannot: I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor (Psalm 140:12). Solomon prays that He would do it for a praying nation: Then hear thou in heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause (1 Kings 8:45). The word belongs to a defender who takes a case in hand and does not let it fall.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MAINTAIN as to hold, preserve or keep in any particular state or condition; to support; to sustain; to defend; to vindicate; to justify by argument.

expand to see more

MAINTAIN, v.t. — To hold, preserve or keep in any particular state or condition; to support; to sustain.

To hold; to keep; not to lose or surrender; as, to maintain a place or post.

To continue; to keep up; not to suffer to cease; as, to maintain a conversation.

To support with food, clothing and other conveniences; as, to maintain a family.

To vindicate; to justify; to defend by argument; as, to maintain one’s cause. From Latin manu tenere, to hold in the hand.

Key Scripture

Titus 3:8 — "This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men."

Titus 3:14 — "And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful."

Psalm 140:12 — "I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor."

1 Kings 8:45 — "Then hear thou in heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause."

Modern Corruption

Titus 3 puts the strongest denial of works-righteousness three verses before the strongest charge to maintain good works, and both halves are routinely lost, each by a different party.

expand to see more

Titus 3:5 says plainly that He saved us not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy, and Titus 3:8 immediately charges believers to be careful to maintain good works. The Reformation held both without embarrassment, and the formula is old: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. Rome’s error at Trent was to make works part of the ground of justification, which destroys the assurance the gospel gives; the antinomian error is to treat the denial in verse 5 as though it made the command in verse 8 optional, which destroys the evidence the gospel produces. James 2 and Titus 3 say the same thing from opposite directions. The 1689 Confession states the balance precisely: good works are the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith, and by them believers manifest their thankfulness — not procure their pardon.

The second half of the verb is worth pressing. Paul does not say perform good works but maintain them, and the qualifier in verse 14 is for necessary uses — useful, ordinary, sustained provision for real needs, not conspicuous acts. That is a different vision of Christian usefulness from the one that measures a church by its programmes and campaigns. Psalm 140:12 supplies the ground under it: the LORD maintains the cause of the afflicted and the right of the poor, and the believer who maintains good works is doing in a small way what God does in a large one. The word belongs to defenders who take a case in hand and do not let it drop.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek proistemi (G4291), to stand before, to maintain or practise diligently; Hebrew asah din, to execute judgment; mishpat (H4941), judgment, the right of a cause.

expand to see more

Greek proistemi (G4291) — to stand before, to preside, and so to maintain or practise; careful to maintain good works (Titus 3:8, 3:14).

Hebrew din (H1777) — to plead a cause, to execute judgment; the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted (Psalm 140:12).

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice, the right belonging to a cause (Psalm 140:12).

Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do or execute; used with mishpat for maintaining a people’s cause (1 Kings 8:45).

Greek akarpos (G175) — unfruitful, barren; the condition Titus 3:14 is written to prevent.

Usage

"Careful to maintain good works (Titus 3:8) — three verses after the strongest denial of works-righteousness in the epistle."

"Maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful (Titus 3:14) — useful and sustained, not conspicuous."

"The LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted (Psalm 140:12) — a defender who takes a case in hand and does not let it fall."
